is a temporary reaction to falling oil
prices and hedging decay rather than a genuine market re-rating, cautioning that a massive options expiration on Friday will leave markets exposed.

Friday's nearly multi-trillion dollar options expiration "strips the dealer gamma that has been pinning realized vol[atility] at an anomalously low 8.75," shifting next week into a "lower-conviction, flow-driven environment without that structural stabilizer," he wrote in a social media post.

In options trading, dealer gamma acts as a shock absorber; when dealers are positioned this way, their automatic hedging activity (that is, buying on dips and selling on rallies to remain neutral) suppresses price swings and keeps volatility artificially low. Once Friday's expiration wipes those positions off the board, that stabilizer vanishes, leaving the market vulnerable to potentially more erratic movements.
Although major stock index futures rallied over 1% Thursday alongside a slide in Brent crude
down over 3% to $102.40 per barrel and WTI
below $100, Shapiro described the relief as "fragile," particularly after Congress
for 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian crude.

The market setup is further pressured by a hawkish Federal Reserve. Shapiro noted that the central bank is "no longer treating the Middle East energy shock as transitory," interpreting recent policy signals as a proactive tightening cycle instead of a "one-and-done" adjustment.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh reinforced that policy stance during his post-meeting press conference Wednesday,

that officials "removed a dose of accommodation." The central banker added that the Fed "must be confident that underlying inflation is moving toward our goal at sufficient speed," noting that this criterion has not yet been met.

Characterizing the current market regime as "fragile," Shapiro advised investors to "lean cautiously bearish into post-expiration" and wait for the gamma roll to clear before taking on new directional risk.
